props.title: Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde
props.initialSlug: Mad scientist's female alter ego turns deadly

sections.content: Hammer Films' gender-bending twist on Stevenson's classic tale marks a fascinating intersection of horror and sexual politics. Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde (1971) brilliantly casts Ralph Bates and Martine Beswick as the dual lead, pushing boundaries by linking Jekyll's transformations to Victorian-era murders. The film cleverly weaves in Jack the Ripper and Burke and Hare, creating a rich tapestry of historical horror that builds on earlier adaptations like Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde (1931) and The Two Faces of Dr. Jekyll (1960).

movies.title: Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde
movies.slug: Hammer Horror's gender-swapped take features Ralph Bates transforming into Martine Beswick while investigating immortality

sections.content: The 1970s marked a crucial shift in horror's treatment of gender and sexuality. While Daughters of Darkness (1971) and The Vampire Lovers (1970) explored similar themes through a vampire lens, Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde stands out for directly confronting Victorian sexual repression through its protagonist's literal gender transformation. Director Roy Ward Baker, fresh from The Vampire Lovers, brings Hammer's trademark gothic atmosphere while pushing into more transgressive territory.

The film's influence ripples through later gender-focused horror, from Sleepaway Camp (1983) to The Silence of the Lambs (1991). Its mixing of historical figures with fiction predates similar approaches in From Hell (2001) and The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen (2003), while its body horror elements connect to later Cronenberg works like Dead Ringers (1988). sections.content: The film's 1970s feminist context adds fascinating layers to its Victorian setting. While earlier Jekyll adaptations focused on male duality, Sister Hyde introduces questions of gender power dynamics that resonate with contemporary films like Lady Macbeth (2016) and The Handmaiden (2016). The movie's blend of historical murder cases with supernatural transformation creates a unique commentary on gender roles and power in Victorian society.
